6.01.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what do you ask a plexus patient?"
- "How did it happen, how long ago, how bad is the pain?"
- "What can the arm do now, and is it getting better?"
- "Birth palsy: the delivery, the weight, when the biceps came back."

### Mechanism
| Story | Think of |
|---|---|
| Motorbike fall; shoulder down, neck bent away | upper roots (C5–C6) torn |
| Arm pulled up hard | lower roots (C8–T1) torn |
| Difficult birth, shoulder dystocia | upper trunk — Erb palsy |
| Breech birth, arm pulled up | lower plexus — Klumpke palsy |
| Wound, axillary surgery | cords or branches, often with the artery |

- Motorbike: the commonest cause; high energy → more avulsion (Miller)
- Birth risks: big baby, dystocia, forceps, diabetic mother

[[FIG: Fig 6.1 — Shoulder down, neck bent away; flail arm · 6.01

### Time since injury
| Time | What it changes |
|---|---|
| First days | life first (ATLS); chart power, sensation |
| 3 months | watch recovery; nerve studies after 4–6 weeks (Miller) |
| 6 months | nerve repair does worse after this (Exam Techniques) |
| Over 1 year (adult) | tendon transfer or fusion, not nerve repair |

- ATLS = Advanced Trauma Life Support
- Ask: is power coming back? Tinel moving down = regrowth

### Pain and function
- Burning pain in a numb arm → root avulsion (deafferentation pain)
- **Painful anaesthetic limb** is a poor sign

| Palsy | Function (Exam Techniques) |
|---|---|
| Upper roots | good hand; no stable shoulder, no elbow flexion |
| Lower roots | good shoulder and elbow; useless hand |

#### Ask every time
| Complaint | Ask |
|---|---|
| Mechanism | traction, birth, wound, operation |
| Time | date of injury; any recovery since? |
| Pain | burning in a numb arm? Sleep? |
| Function | dominance, job, what the arm does |
| Other injuries | head, neck, chest, vessels |

- **Red flags:** cold pale hand → vascular injury; leg weakness → cord injury
- **Memory:** four questions — how, when, pain, function
- General interview → ch 1

6.02.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "examine this brachial plexus"
- "Standing: look front, side, behind, and the face for Horner."
- "Feel bones, pulse, sweating; Tinel in the neck; muscles top to bottom."
- "Sensation, reflexes; then spine, shoulder, legs for long tract signs."

- **Whole brachial plexus exam (video):** [▶ Lennard Funk · 5:46](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WBDpXuL78Fg)

### The route on one page
| Position | What you do (in order) |
|---|---|
| Standing — front | Look: attitude, wasting, Horner, scars, clavicle |
| Standing — behind | Look: winging; Special: rhomboids, serratus, trapezius |
| Standing — behind | Move: supraspinatus, infraspinatus, subscapularis |
| Standing — front | Move: pectoralis heads, latissimus cough, deltoid |
| Sitting | Feel: bones, pulses, sweating; Tinel above the clavicle |
| Sitting | Neuro: myotomes C5–T1, branches (MRC grade), dermatomes, reflexes |
| Finish | pulses, cervical spine, shoulder, legs for long tract signs |

- **Memory:** Look, Feel, Move, Measure, Special · then Neuro, Vascular, Joints above/below
- **Memory:** muscles top to bottom — **2-1-3-5**: 2 root nerves, 1 trunk nerve, 3 cord muscles, 5 branches

### Standing — look
- Expose to the waist; look from the front, side and behind
- Cannot stand → avulsion may have injured the cord

| Look for | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Attitude** | waiter's tip → Erb; claw → Klumpke; flail → total |
| **Wasting** | deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, small hand muscles |
| **Horner syndrome** | ptosis, small pupil → T1 avulsion (6.4) |
| **Scars** | neck, clavicle, axilla |
| **Bruising** | deep in the posterior triangle → preganglionic (McRae) |

[[FIG: Fig 6.2 — Spinati wasting; look into the axilla · 6.02

### Sitting — feel
| Feel | Why |
|---|---|
| Bones | fracture of neck, clavicle, scapula, first rib |
| Pulses | radial, brachial — the artery runs with the plexus |
| Sweating | dry skin → nerve cut (→ ch 5) |
| Above the clavicle | Tinel along the roots |

[[FIG: Fig 6.3 — Numb skin above the clavicle → C3–C4 also hit → poor outlook (McRae) · 6.02
[[FIG: Fig 6.8 — Radial pulse checked in every plexus case · 6.02

### Sitting — move (top to bottom)
| Level | Nerve (roots) | Muscle → test |
|---|---|---|
| Roots | dorsal scapular (C5) | rhomboids → elbow back |
| Roots | long thoracic (C5–C7) | serratus anterior → wall push |
| Upper trunk | suprascapular (C5–C6) | supra- and infraspinatus → feel both fossae |
| Lateral cord | lateral pectoral (C5–C7) | pectoralis major, clavicular head |
| Medial cord | medial pectoral (C8–T1) | pectoralis major, sternal head |
| Posterior cord | thoracodorsal (C6–C8) | latissimus dorsi → cough test |
| Posterior cord | subscapular (C5–C6) | subscapularis → lift-off |
| Branches | axillary, musculocutaneous, radial, median, ulnar | deltoid, biceps, triceps, FDP, interossei |

- FDP = flexor digitorum profundus; MRC = Medical Research Council grade; branches → ch 5
- Test trapezius too: the accessory nerve lies near the trunks

[[FIG: Fig 6.10 — Quick hand screen: point, cross fingers, make an O · 6.02

### Sitting — sensation and reflexes
- Pinwheel, then light touch; compare the sound side
- Dermatome pattern → root or trunk; nerve pattern → cord or branch (Exam Techniques)

| Spot | Root |
|---|---|
| Shoulder tip | supraclavicular nerves (C3–C4) |
| Axillary floor | intercostobrachial (T2) |
| Key spots, root by root | → ch 9 (9.3) |

- **Memory:** "elbow: C5 out, T1 in; fingers: thumb C6, middle C7, little C8"
- **Memory:** "5-6 pick up sticks (biceps), 7-8 lay them straight (triceps)"

- Neck, Spurling → root compression (→ ch 9); legs → long tract signs (Nagah)

- Starting distal misses the root branches that decide pre- versus post-ganglionic
- Say → "**I test the scapular muscles first, then go down the limb.**"

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "where is the lesion?"
- "Three answers: level, extent, prognosis (Exam Techniques)."
- "Level: above or below the clavicle; if above, pre- or post-ganglionic."
- "Clinical examination gets the site right in only about 60%."

- **Memory:** **LEP** — Level, Extent, Prognosis

### Build the plexus — 5-3-6-3-5
| Part | Number | Where | Key branch → muscle |
|---|---|---|---|
| Roots | 5 (C5–T1) | between the scalenes | dorsal scapular → rhomboids; long thoracic → serratus |
| Trunks | 3 | posterior triangle | suprascapular → spinati |
| Divisions | 6 | behind the clavicle | none |
| Cords | 3 | around the axillary artery | pectorals, latissimus, subscapularis |
| Branches | 5 | axilla and arm | musculocutaneous, axillary, radial, median, ulnar |

- **Memory:** "Randy Travis Drinks Cold Beer" — roots, trunks, divisions, cords, branches
- Above the clavicle = roots and trunks; below = cords and branches (Exam Techniques)

### Pre- or post-ganglionic?
| Sign | Pre-ganglionic (avulsion) | Post-ganglionic (rupture) |
|---|---|---|
| Horner syndrome | present (T1) | absent |
| Rhomboids, serratus | paralysed | working |
| Phrenic (chest X-ray) | high hemidiaphragm | normal |
| Tinel in the neck | absent | present (McRae) |
| Histamine flare in numb skin | kept | lost (McRae) |
| Sensory nerve action potential | normal in a numb arm | absent (Miller) |
| Outlook | no recovery → nerve transfer | repair or graft possible |

- **Memory:** pre-ganglionic = numb skin, live axons — the ganglion keeps them alive
- Flare kept after 3 weeks in numb skin → pre-ganglionic certain (McRae)
- Transverse process fracture on X-ray → avulsion likely (Miller)

6.04.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "the plexus tests"
- "Before the ganglion: Horner, rhomboids, serratus, Tinel."
- "Trunk: suprascapular. Cords: pectoralis heads, latissimus. Then grade every muscle."

### Is the root torn from the cord?
#### Horner signs check
- **Aim:** sympathetic loss from T1 avulsion
- **How:** in good light, compare both lids, pupils and brows
- **Positive:** ptosis, small pupil, dry skin, sunken eye → T1 avulsed
- **Why:** sympathetic fibres leave T1 just outside the foramen
- **Trap:** unequal pupils after trauma are not always head injury
- **Video:** [▶ Sam Tapsell · 5:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JBVGh0gyyYc)

[[FIG: Fig 6.15 — Horner: ptosis, small pupil, sunken eye · 6.04

HIGH YIELD — Memory hook
- **PMAE** — Ptosis, Miosis, Anhidrosis, Enophthalmos

#### Rhomboid test
- **Aim:** dorsal scapular nerve (C5) — the first root branch
- **How:** hand on the hip; you push the elbow forward; feel the rhomboids
- **Positive:** no contraction → above the upper trunk → avulsion likely (McRae)
- **Why:** the nerve leaves C5 just outside the foramen
- **Video:** [▶ Physiotutors · 1:21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gn3s7sVtyWo)

[[FIG: Fig 6.16 — Rhomboids: elbow pushed back against resistance · 6.04

#### Serratus wall push test (plexus)
- **Aim:** long thoracic nerve (C5–C7) — root branch
- **How:** technique → ch 5
- **Positive:** medial border lifts off the chest → root-level lesion
- **Trap:** a flail arm cannot push; hold the arm up (McRae)
- **Video:** [▶ Physiotutors · 1:22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jatVx3v7qDI)

[[FIG: Fig 6.17 — Wall push: the medial border wings · 6.04

#### Tinel over the supraclavicular fossa
- **Aim:** rupture or avulsion of each root
- **How:** tap firmly down the side of the neck along the roots
- **Positive:** tingling in that dermatome → root ruptured (post-ganglionic)
- **Why:** a torn stump fires; an avulsed root has left the neck
- **Trap:** sometimes positive even with an avulsion (McRae)
- **Video:** [▶ CRTechnologies · 0:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E6DUQB9i8O4)

[[FIG: Fig 6.18 — Tinel: tingling runs distally · 6.04

### Is the upper trunk working?
#### Suprascapular nerve test
- **Aim:** suprascapular nerve (C5–C6) from the upper trunk
- **How:** resist abduction, then external rotation; feel both fossae
- **Positive:** hollow, silent fossae → upper trunk or nerve lesion
- **Why:** first branch after the trunk forms — a level marker
- **Trap:** a cuff tear also weakens it; feel the muscle
- **Video:** [▶ AMBOSS · 1:45](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=R67cIKM3EAM)

[[FIG: Fig 6.19 — Feeling the spinati; wasting from palsy · 6.04

### Which cord is hit?
#### Pectoralis clavicular versus sternal head
- **Aim:** lateral cord (C5–C7) versus medial cord (C8–T1)
- **How:** forward flexion for the clavicular head; waist squeeze for the sternal
- **Positive:** clavicular head lost → lateral cord; sternal lost → medial cord
- **Why:** lateral pectoral nerve → clavicular head; medial pectoral → sternal
- **Video:** [▶ Western Tech PTA · 2:42](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=afkrc67fIM0)

[[FIG: Fig 6.20 — Pectoralis major: hands on the waist, squeeze in · 6.04

#### Latissimus cough test
- **Aim:** thoracodorsal nerve, posterior cord
- **How:** you grasp both posterior axillary folds; patient coughs
- **Positive:** no twitch on one side → posterior cord lesion
- **Why:** latissimus helps forced breathing
- **Video:** [▶ Physiotutors · 1:20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BIQtRi0-ECQ)

[[FIG: Fig 6.21 — Latissimus: push down and back · 6.04

### How strong is each level?
#### Key muscles by level
- Grade each with MRC → ch 1 (1.4)

| Key muscle | Root |
|---|---|
| Deltoid | C5 |
| Biceps | C5–C6 |
| Wrist extensors | C6–C7 |
| Triceps | C7 |
| FDP | C8 |
| Interossei | T1 |

#### Myotome screen
- **Aim:** which roots work, in six movements
- **How:** resist shoulder abduction, elbow flexion and extension, wrist, fingers, spread
- **Positive:** a lost movement → that root is out (table below)
- **Why:** each movement maps to one or two roots
- **Video:** [▶ John Gibbons · 3:20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=a4_RPLsaoRM)

[[FIG: Fig 6.22 — The six myotome movements, C5 to T1 · 6.04

| Movement | Root (Nagah) |
|---|---|
| Shoulder abduction | C5 |
| Elbow flexion | C5–C6 |
| Elbow and finger extension | C7–C8 |
| Finger flexion | C8–T1 |
| Finger spread (intrinsics) | T1 |

| Trapezius shrug | weak → trunk-level lesion (→ ch 5) |
| Histamine (triple response) | flare kept in numb skin → pre-ganglionic |

6.05.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "two-minute plexus short case"
- "Spot: attitude, wasting, Horner, scars. Do: rhomboids, serratus, myotomes."
- "Say: level, pre or post-ganglionic, and one differential."

### Erb palsy (adult or obstetric)
- **Spot:** waiter's tip — adducted, internally rotated, elbow straight, pronated
- **Do:** deltoid, cuff, biceps lost; rhomboids, serratus usually spared (McRae)
- **Say:** "Upper trunk (C5–C6) palsy. Differential: C5–C6 root avulsion."

[[FIG: Fig 6.24 — Waiter's tip posture · 6.05

### Klumpke palsy
- **Spot:** claw hand, wasted small muscles, forearm supinated (Exam Techniques)
- **Do:** numb medial forearm; look for Horner
- **Say:** "Lower trunk (C8–T1) palsy. Differential: cervical rib or apical tumour."

[[FIG: Fig 6.25 — Claw hand; T1 alone wastes the thenar group too · 6.05

### Total plexus palsy (flail arm)
- **Spot:** flail, numb, wasted arm; Horner; supinated claw hand
- **Do:** rhomboids, serratus, Tinel in the neck; ask about burning
- **Say:** "Total plexus palsy, pre-ganglionic. Differential: mixed avulsion and rupture."

[[FIG: Fig 6.26 — Old total palsy: wasting, clawing, Horner · 6.05

### Infraclavicular (cord-level) lesion
- **Spot:** axillary scar; scapular muscles normal
- **Do:** nerve-pattern numbness; radial pulse — the artery runs with the cords
- **Say:** "Infraclavicular cord lesion. Differential: several peripheral nerve injuries."

[[FIG: Fig 6.27 — Single-nerve sensory loss · 6.05

### Late obstetric palsy
- **Spot:** child, small arm, internally rotated, no external rotation
- **Do:** passive external rotation in adduction; trumpet sign on hand to mouth
- **Do:** feel the head behind — posterior dislocation, even by 2 years (Campbell)
- **Say:** "Old obstetric palsy, internal rotation contracture. Differential: posterior dislocation."

[[FIG: Fig 6.28 — Modified Mallet score of shoulder function · 6.05

| Obstetric numbers (Campbell) | Value |
|---|---|
| Spontaneous recovery | 66–92% |
| No deltoid or biceps by | 3–6 months → explore |
| Toronto score at 3 months | ≤3.5 → microsurgery |

PITFALL — "an infant arm that will not move is always plexus palsy"
- Clavicle or humeral fracture and septic shoulder cause pseudoparalysis (Campbell)
- Say → "**Fracture pseudoparalysis settles in 10–21 days; weak at 1 month → plexus.**"

6.06.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "present your case"
- "Who, mechanism, time; findings top to bottom; then level, type and prognosis."
- "Always say pre- or post-ganglionic, and why."

### Present it like this
| Part | Say |
|---|---|
| History | "A 25-year-old motorcyclist, right arm weak and numb, 4 months." |
| Look | "Flail right arm, shoulder girdle wasting, right Horner." |
| Roots | "Rhomboids and serratus paralysed; no Tinel in the neck." |
| Below | "No power and dermatomal numbness, C5 to T1." |
| Verdict | "Total palsy, pre-ganglionic, poor prognosis; CT myelography next." |

[[FIG: Fig 6.29 — Chart the numb area on a drawing · 6.06

### Differential of a weak, numb arm
| Group | Examples |
|---|---|
| Neck | cervical root or cord lesion |
| Outlet | cervical rib, apical (Pancoast) tumour |
| Plexus | traction, birth, radiation neuritis |
| Nerve | single or several nerves (→ ch 5) |
| Shoulder | cuff tear, posterior dislocation |

- **Memory:** work down the arm — neck, outlet, plexus, nerve, shoulder

### The Examiner Asks
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Why Horner means avulsion? | sympathetic fibres leave T1 near the foramen |
| First nerves off the roots? | dorsal scapular, long thoracic |
| Tinel positive in the neck? | rupture — repairable root |
| Why is sensory conduction normal in avulsion? | ganglion keeps the sensory axon alive |
| Supraclavicular versus infraclavicular? | roots and trunks versus cords and branches |
| Commonest adult patterns? | C5–C6; C5–C7; C5–T1 (McRae) |
| Obstetric palsy: when explore? | no biceps by 3–6 months |

6.07.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "the whole plexus on one page"
- "Look, feel, Tinel, muscles top to bottom (2-1-3-5), sensation, reflexes."
- "Answer level, extent, prognosis."

### OSCE cards in one table
| Test | Position | Positive means |
|---|---|---|
| Horner signs check | Sitting | ptosis, small pupil → T1 avulsion |
| Rhomboid test | Standing, behind | no contraction → above the upper trunk |
| Serratus wall push (plexus) | Standing, behind | winging → root-level lesion |
| Tinel over the supraclavicular fossa | Sitting | tingling in dermatome → rupture |
| Suprascapular nerve test | Standing, behind | no contraction → upper trunk lesion |
| Pectoralis clavicular versus sternal head | Standing, front | clavicular → lateral cord; sternal → medial |
| Latissimus cough test | Standing, front | no twitch → posterior cord |
| MRC power grading (→ ch 1) | Sitting | 0–5 per muscle → record recovery |
| Myotome screen | Sitting | lost movement → that root |
